plain_english: The ruling part of your mind, when it's working right, stays flexible toward whatever happens in the world. It can easily shift to what's actually possible when its first plan doesn't work out. It never locks itself completely onto one goal. Whatever it's working toward, it holds lightly — ready to change course. When things go against what it first wanted, it makes that setback into its new material to work with. It's like fire meeting obstacles in its path. A small fire gets put out by what blocks it. But a big fire turns everything into fuel. It consumes whatever gets in its way and grows stronger from it.
original_excerpt: That inward mistress part of man if it be in its own true natural temper, is towards all worldly chances and events ever so disposed and affected, that it will easily turn and apply itself to that which may be, and is within its own power to compass, when that cannot be which at first it intended. For it never doth absolutely addict and apply itself to any one object, but whatsoever it is that it doth now intend and prosecute, it doth prosecute it with exception and reservation; so that whatsoever it is that falls out contrary to its first intentions, even that afterwards it makes its proper object. Even as the fire when it prevails upon those things that are in his way; by which things indeed a little fire would have been quenched, but a great fire doth soon turn to its own nature, and so consume whatsoever comes in his way: yea by those very things it is made greater and greater.

plain_english: Don't do anything hastily or carelessly. Do everything according to the most precise and perfect principles.
original_excerpt: Let nothing be done rashly, and at random, but all things according to the most exact and perfect rules of art.

plain_english: People look for private places to escape to — country villages, the seashore, mountains. You yourself often crave such places. But you should know this comes from the simplest kind of thinking. You can retire into yourself whenever you want, and find rest there, free from all troubles. No one can retreat to a better place than his own soul. This is especially true if he has already prepared good things within himself. When he turns inward to look, he can immediately find perfect peace and calm. By calm I mean a proper, orderly state of mind, free from all confusion and chaos. Give yourself this retreat constantly, and refresh yourself through it. Keep these ideas brief and basic. As soon as you remember them, they should be enough to cleanse your soul completely. Then you can return to whatever you were doing, pleased with those things, after this short withdrawal into yourself.
original_excerpt: They seek for themselves private retiring places, as country villages, the sea-shore, mountains; yea thou thyself art wont to long much after such places. But all this thou must know proceeds from simplicity in the highest degree. At what time soever thou wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and free from all businesses. A man cannot any whither retire better than to his own soul; he especially who is beforehand provided of such things within, which whensoever he doth withdraw himself to look in, may presently afford unto him perfect ease and tranquillity. By tranquillity I understand a decent orderly disposition and carriage, free from all confusion and tumultuousness. Afford then thyself this retiring continually, and thereby refresh and renew thyself. Let these precepts be brief and fundamental, which as soon as thou dost call them to mind, may suffice thee to purge thy soul throughly, and to send thee away well pleased with those things whatsoever they be, which now again after this short withdrawing of thy soul into herself thou dost return unto.

plain_english: What are you upset about? Are you offended by people's bad behavior? Remember that all thinking beings were made to help each other. It's part of justice to put up with them. They don't mean to do wrong. And think about this — how many people who once fought bitterly, who hated and suspected each other, are now long dead and turned to ash? It's time to let it go.
original_excerpt: For what is it that thou art offended at? Can it be at the wickedness of men, when thou dost call to mind this conclusion, that all reasonable creatures are made one for another? and that it is part of justice to bear with them? and that it is against their wills that they offend? and how many already, who once likewise prosecuted their enmities, suspected, hated, and fiercely contended, are now long ago stretched out, and reduced unto ashes? It is time for thee to make an end.

plain_english: When things happen to you in life, can you really be upset about them? Remember our choice: either the universe has a plan, or it's just random atoms colliding. Either way, we proved that the whole world is like one city. As for your body, what is there to fear? Your mind, once it remembers its own strength, doesn't care whether life goes smoothly or roughly. It stays detached. You've heard this before about pain and pleasure. But maybe worry about your reputation still distracts you?
original_excerpt: As for those things which among the common chances of the world happen unto thee as thy particular lot and portion, canst thou be displeased with any of them, when thou dost call that our ordinary dilemma to mind, either a providence, or Democritus his atoms; and with it, whatsoever we brought to prove that the whole world is as it were one city? And as for thy body, what canst thou fear, if thou dost consider that thy mind and understanding, when once it hath recollected itself, and knows its own power, hath in this life and breath (whether it run smoothly and gently, or whether harshly and rudely), no interest at all, but is altogether indifferent: and whatsoever else thou hast heard and assented unto concerning either pain or pleasure? But the care of thine honour and reputation will perchance distract thee?

plain_english: How can any of this matter when you look back and see how quickly everything gets forgotten? Think about the endless chaos of time before us and after us. Think about how empty praise really is. Think about how people's opinions shift and change. Think about how small the place is where this all happens. The whole earth is just a dot. The part we live on is tiny. And of that tiny part, how many people are there who might praise you? What kind of people are they anyway? What's left then is to practice pulling back into yourself often. Most important of all, don't let yourself get scattered. Don't chase after anything too hard. Stay free and look at everything simply. Remember you're someone whose goal is virtue. Remember you're someone whose nature is to be kind and connected to others. You're a citizen. You're going to die.
original_excerpt: How can that be, if thou dost look back, and consider both how quickly all things that are, are forgotten, and what an immense chaos of eternity was before, and will follow after all things: and the vanity of praise, and the inconstancy and variableness of human judgments and opinions, and the narrowness of the place, wherein it is limited and circumscribed? For the whole earth is but as one point; and of it, this inhabited part of it, is but a very little part; and of this part, how many in number, and what manner of men are they, that will commend thee? What remains then, but that thou often put in practice this kind of retiring of thyself, to this little part of thyself; and above all things, keep thyself from distraction, and intend not anything vehemently, but be free and consider all things, as a man whose proper object is Virtue, as a man whose true nature is to be kind and sociable, as a citizen, as a mortal creature.

plain_english: Among other things you can use to pull yourself back, keep these two close at hand. First, that things themselves don't reach your soul. They stay outside, quiet and still. All the noise and trouble comes from your opinions about them. Second, that everything you see now will change very soon and be gone. Remember how many changes you have already witnessed in your lifetime. This world is nothing but change, and this life is just opinion.
original_excerpt: Among other things, which to consider, and look into thou must use to withdraw thyself, let those two be among the most obvious and at hand. One, that the things or objects themselves reach not unto the soul, but stand without still and quiet, and that it is from the opinion only which is within, that all the tumult and all the trouble doth proceed. The next, that all these things, which now thou seest, shall within a very little while be changed, and be no more: and ever call to mind, how many changes and alterations in the world thou thyself hast already been an eyewitness of in thy time. This world is mere change, and this life, opinion.

plain_english: If all people can understand and think clearly, then the ability to reason is shared by everyone. If reasoning is universal, then the part of reason that tells us what to do and what not to do is also shared. If that's true, then law is shared. If law is shared, then we are all fellow citizens. If we are fellow citizens, then we belong to one common state. If that's so, then the world is like a single city. What other state could include all people as members? From this shared city we get our understanding, our reason, and our laws. Where else could they come from? Just as the earthy part of me comes from common earth, and the wet part comes from water, and my breath and life have their source, and the dry and fiery parts in me have their origin — nothing comes from nowhere, and nothing becomes nothing — so my understanding must also come from some shared source.
original_excerpt: If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all. If reason is general, then is that reason also, which prescribeth what is to be done and what not, common unto all. If that, then law. If law, then are we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one commonweal. If so, then the world is as it were a city. For which other commonweal is it, that all men can be said to be members of? From this common city it is, that understanding, reason, and law is derived unto us, for from whence else? For as that which in me is earthly I have from some common earth; and that which is moist from some other element is imparted; as my breath and life hath its proper fountain; and that likewise which is dry and fiery in me: (for there is nothing which doth not proceed from something; as also there is nothing that can be reduced unto mere nothing:) so also is there some common beginning from whence my understanding hath proceeded.

plain_english: Birth is natural, and so is death — both are part of nature's wisdom. We are made of elements that return to the same elements when we die. No one should be ashamed of this. It's just one event in a series of things that happen to thinking creatures like us. It's not wrong or out of place. It fits with how humans are naturally made.
original_excerpt: As generation is, so also death, a secret of nature's wisdom: a mixture of elements, resolved into the same elements again, a thing surely which no man ought to be ashamed of: in a series of other fatal events and consequences, which a rational creature is subject unto, not improper or incongruous, nor contrary to the natural and proper constitution of man himself.

plain_english: These things happen for these reasons. They have to happen. Someone who doesn't want these things to happen is like someone who wants a fig tree to grow without sap. Remember this: very soon, both you and he will be dead. And soon after that, even your names will be forgotten.
original_excerpt: Such and such things, from such and such causes, must of necessity proceed. He that would not have such things to happen, is as he that would have the fig-tree grow without any sap or moisture. In sum, remember this, that within a very little while, both thou and he shall both be dead, and after a little while more, not so much as your names and memories shall be remaining.

plain_english: Take away opinion, and no one will think they've been wronged. If no one thinks they've been wronged, then there is no such thing as wrong. What doesn't make a person worse cannot make his life worse. It cannot hurt him inside or out. Nature made it this way because it had to be so.
original_excerpt: Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged. If no man shall think himself wronged, then is there no more any such thing as wrong. That which makes not man himself the worse, cannot make his life the worse, neither can it hurt him either inwardly or outwardly. It was expedient in nature that it should be so, and therefore necessary.

plain_english: Whatever happens in the world happens justly. If you pay close attention, you will see this. I don't just mean things follow in logical order. I mean they happen according to true justice, like fair distribution based on what everything truly deserves. Keep noticing this, as you have started to do. Whatever you do, make sure it's something a truly good person would do. Watch for this in every action.
original_excerpt: Whatsoever doth happen in the world, doth happen justly, and so if thou dost well take heed, thou shalt find it. I say not only in right order by a series of inevitable consequences, but according to justice and as it were by way of equal distribution, according to the true worth of everything. Continue then to take notice of it, as thou hast begun, and whatsoever thou dost, do it not without this proviso, that it be a thing of that nature that a good man (as the word good is properly taken) may do it. This observe carefully in every action.

plain_english: Don't accept the twisted ideas of someone who wrongs you, or let them shape how you see things. Look at the situation itself and see what it really is.
original_excerpt: Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth, or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see what it is in very truth.

plain_english: Keep these two rules ready at all times. First, do nothing unless your reason — that royal part of your mind — tells you it will help other people. Second, if someone can correct you or show you where you're wrong, be ready to change your mind. Don't change because it feels good or makes you look better. Change only when you see real evidence of what's right, or what serves the common good, or some other worthy reason.
original_excerpt: These two rules, thou must have always in a readiness. First, do nothing at all, but what reason proceeding from that regal and supreme part, shall for the good and benefit of men, suggest unto thee. And secondly, if any man that is present shall be able to rectify thee or to turn thee from some erroneous persuasion, that thou be always ready to change thy mind, and this change to proceed, not from any respect of any pleasure or credit thereon depending, but always from some probable apparent ground of justice, or of some public good thereby to be furthered; or from some other such inducement.

plain_english: Do you have reason? I do. Then why don't you use it? If your reason does its job, what more could you need?
original_excerpt: Hast thou reason? I have. Why then makest thou not use of it? For if thy reason do her part, what more canst thou require?

plain_english: Until now you have existed as a separate part. Soon you will dissolve back into the common substance of the one who first created you. Or rather, you will return to that original rational substance from which everything else came. Many small pieces of incense are placed on the same altar. One burns up first, then another. In the end, it all comes to the same thing.
original_excerpt: As a part hitherto thou hast had a particular subsistence: and now shalt thou vanish away into the common substance of Him, who first begot thee, or rather thou shalt be resumed again into that original rational substance, out of which all others have issued, and are propagated. Many small pieces of frankincense are set upon the same altar, one drops first and is consumed, another after; and it comes all to one.

plain_english: In ten days, if it happens, you'll be seen as a god by the same people who right now would think of you as nothing more than a dumb animal or an ape—if you went back to old beliefs and stopped honoring reason.
original_excerpt: Within ten days, if so happen, thou shalt be esteemed a god of them, who now if thou shalt return to the dogmata and to the honouring of reason, will esteem of thee no better than of a mere brute, and of an ape.

plain_english: Not as if you had thousands of years to live. Death hangs over you. While you are still alive, while you can, be good.
original_excerpt: Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live. Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.

plain_english: How much time and peace you gain when you don't worry about what your neighbor said, did, or tried to do. Focus only on your own actions — that they may be just and good. As Agathos said: Don't look around at the faults of others, but run straight ahead without getting distracted or agitated.
original_excerpt: Now much time and leisure doth he gain, who is not curious to know what his neighbour hath said, or hath done, or hath attempted, but only what he doth himself, that it may be just and holy? or to express it in Agathos' words, Not to look about upon the evil conditions of others, but to run on straight in the line, without any loose and extravagant agitation.

plain_english:
Someone who craves fame and wants to be remembered after death doesn't think this through. The people who remember him will soon die too. And the people who come after them will also die. Eventually all memory of him will disappear completely. This chain of people admiring him and then dying will finally end.

But let's say the people who remember you and your memory itself could last forever. What good would that do you? I won't even ask what good it does after you're dead. What good does praise do you even while you're alive? It only helps for practical reasons — what we might call good management.
original_excerpt: He who is greedy of credit and reputation after his death, doth not consider, that they themselves by whom he is remembered, shall soon after every one of them be dead; and they likewise that succeed those; until at last all memory, which hitherto by the succession of men admiring and soon after dying hath had its course, be quite extinct. But suppose that both they that shall remember thee, and thy memory with them should be immortal, what is that to thee? I will not say to thee after thou art dead; but even to thee living, what is thy praise? But only for a secret and politic consideration, which we call οἰκονομίαν, or dispensation.

plain_english: Whatever good qualities you have that come naturally to you — let's set that aside for now, since we're talking about something else. Anything that is truly beautiful or good is beautiful and good in itself. It doesn't need praise to complete it. So the thing that gets praised isn't made better or worse by the praise. I mean this even for things we usually call beautiful and good — things praised for their materials or skilled craftsmanship. As for what is truly good, what more does it need beyond justice or truth? What more than kindness and humility? Which of these becomes good or beautiful because someone praises it? Or gets damaged when criticized? Does an emerald become worse if no one praises it? Do gold, ivory, or purple fabric? Is there anything — even common things like a knife, a flower, or a tree — that changes based on praise?
original_excerpt: For as for that, that it is the gift of nature, whatsoever is commended in thee, what might be objected from thence, let that now that we are upon another consideration be omitted as unseasonable. That which is fair and goodly, whatsoever it be, and in what respect soever it be, that it is fair and goodly, it is so of itself, and terminates in itself, not admitting praise as a part or member: that therefore which is praised, is not thereby made either better or worse. This I understand even of those things, that are commonly called fair and good, as those which are commended either for the matter itself, or for curious workmanship. As for that which is truly good, what can it stand in need of more than either justice or truth; or more than either kindness and modesty? Which of all those, either becomes good or fair, because commended; or dispraised suffers any damage? Doth the emerald become worse in itself, or more vile if it be not commended? Doth gold, or ivory, or purple? Is there anything that doth though never so common, as a knife, a flower, or a tree?

plain_english: If souls do survive death (as some people claim), how could the air hold them all forever? How could the earth hold all the buried bodies? Here on earth, dead bodies decay and change into something else. This makes room for new bodies. The same thing must happen with souls. After death, they move into the air for a while. Then they change or merge back into the original source that all souls come from. This makes room for new souls that were once joined to bodies and now exist alone.
original_excerpt: If so be that the souls remain after death (say they that will not believe it); how is the air from all eternity able to contain them? How is the earth (say I) ever from that time able to Contain the bodies of them that are buried? For as here the change and resolution of dead bodies into another kind of subsistence (whatsoever it be;) makes place for other dead bodies: so the souls after death transferred into the air, after they have conversed there a while, are either by way of transmutation, or transfusion, or conflagration, received again into that original rational substance, from which all others do proceed: and so give way to those souls, who before coupled and associated unto bodies, now begin to subsist single.

plain_english: This can be explained if we assume souls exist alone for a while after death. Think about this: beyond all the bodies buried in the earth, consider how many animals we and other creatures eat every day. Despite this huge number being consumed and buried in the bodies that eat them, the same space can hold them all. This happens because they transform — some into blood, some into air and fire. What's the real insight here? We must separate things into what receives action (matter) and what gives action (form).
original_excerpt: This, upon a supposition that the souls after death do for a while subsist single, may be answered. And here, (besides the number of bodies, so buried and contained by the earth), we may further consider the number of several beasts, eaten by us men, and by other creatures. For notwithstanding that such a multitude of them is daily consumed, and as it were buried in the bodies of the eaters, yet is the same place and body able to contain them, by reason of their conversion, partly into blood, partly into air and fire. What in these things is the speculation of truth? to divide things into that which is passive and material; and that which is active and formal.

plain_english: Don't get off track. With every impulse and desire, do what is right. And always be careful to see clearly what every thought or impression really is.
original_excerpt: Not to wander out of the way, but upon every motion and desire, to perform that which is just: and ever to be careful to attain to the true natural apprehension of every fancy, that presents itself.

plain_english: Whatever works for you, O World, works for me. Nothing can be out of time for me if it's the right time for you. Whatever your seasons bring, I will always welcome as good fruit. O Nature! All things come from you, exist in you, and return to you. If someone could say of Athens, 'You lovely city of Cecrops,' shouldn't I say of the world, 'You lovely city of God?'
original_excerpt: Whatsoever is expedient unto thee, O World, is expedient unto me; nothing can either be 'unseasonable unto me, or out of date, which unto thee is seasonable. Whatsoever thy seasons bear, shall ever by me be esteemed as happy fruit, and increase. O Nature! from thee are all things, in thee all things subsist, and to thee all tend. Could he say of Athens, Thou lovely city of Cecrops; and shalt not thou say of the world, Thou lovely city of God?

plain_english: People often say, "Don't get involved in too many things if you want to be happy." There's truth in this. The best thing you can do is stick to necessary actions only — the ones that reason commands in someone who knows they were born to live with others. This brings two kinds of happiness: the joy that comes from doing good, and the peace that comes from doing less. Most of what we say and do is unnecessary. Cut these things out and you'll have more time and less trouble. So before each action, ask yourself: "Is this something I actually need to do?" Don't just cut out unnecessary actions — cut out unnecessary thoughts too. When you stop the pointless thinking, you prevent the pointless actions that follow.
original_excerpt: They will say commonly, Meddle not with many things, if thou wilt live cheerfully. Certainly there is nothing better, than for a man to confine himself to necessary actions; to such and so many only, as reason in a creature that knows itself born for society, will command and enjoin. This will not only procure that cheerfulness, which from the goodness, but that also, which from the paucity of actions doth usually proceed. For since it is so, that most of those things, which we either speak or do, are unnecessary; if a man shall cut them off, it must needs follow that he shall thereby gain much leisure, and save much trouble, and therefore at every action a man must privately by way of admonition suggest unto himself, What? may not this that now I go about, be of the number of unnecessary actions? Neither must he use himself to cut off actions only, but thoughts and imaginations also, that are unnecessary for so will unnecessary consequent actions the better be prevented and cut off.

plain_english: Try living like a good person. Someone who accepts whatever happens to him in this world. Someone who is content with doing what's right now and keeping a good heart for the future. See how that feels to you. You have tried the other way of living. Now try this way. Stop troubling yourself from now on. Make your life simple.
original_excerpt: Try also how a good man's life; (of one, who is well pleased with those things whatsoever, which among the common changes and chances of this world fall to his own lot and share; and can live well contented and fully satisfied in the justice of his own proper present action, and in the goodness of his disposition for the future:) will agree with thee. Thou hast had experience of that other kind of life: make now trial of this also. Trouble not thyself any more henceforth, reduce thyself unto perfect simplicity.

plain_english: Does someone offend you? They harm themselves, not you. Why let it bother you? Has something happened to you? Good. Whatever it is, it was meant for you from the beginning of time. It's part of the pattern of everything that has happened or will happen. To sum it all up: life is short. We must make the most of the present moment with wisdom and fairness. Enjoy yourself, but stay balanced.
original_excerpt: Doth any man offend? It is against himself that he doth offend: why should it trouble thee? Hath anything happened unto thee? It is well, whatsoever it be, it is that which of all the common chances of the world from the very beginning in the series of all other things that have, or shall happen, was destinated and appointed unto thee. To comprehend all in a few words, our life is short; we must endeavour to gain the present time with best discretion and justice. Use recreation with sobriety.

plain_english: Either this world is a beautiful, ordered whole — everything arranged and ruled by design. Or even if it's a confused mixture, it's still beautiful. How could there be any beauty in you while the whole world contains nothing but chaos? All things are different from each other by their natural properties. Yet they are spread throughout everything and united by natural connection.
original_excerpt: Either this world is a κόσμος or comely piece, because all disposed and governed by certain order: or if it be a mixture, though confused, yet still it is a comely piece. For is it possible that in thee there should be any beauty at all, and that in the whole world there should be nothing but disorder and confusion? and all things in it too, by natural different properties one from another differenced and distinguished; and yet all through diffused, and by natural sympathy, one to another united, as they are?

plain_english: Some people are cruel or spiteful. Others are weak. Some are harsh and unforgiving. Others are wild and inhuman. Some act like sheep. Others act like children. Some are stupid, dishonest, vulgar, deceptive, or tyrannical. So what? If someone can be a stranger to the world who doesn't understand what's in it, why can't you be a stranger who simply wonders at what happens in it?
original_excerpt: A black or malign disposition, an effeminate disposition; an hard inexorable disposition, a wild inhuman disposition, a sheepish disposition, a childish disposition; a blockish, a false, a scurril, a fraudulent, a tyrannical: what then? If he be a stranger in the world, that knows not the things that are in it; why not be a stranger as well, that wonders at the things that are done in it?

plain_english: The real runaway is the one who flees from reason — the thing that makes us social beings. The truly blind person cannot see with their mind's eye. The truly poor person needs others and lacks everything necessary for life within themselves. Someone who complains about what happens to them becomes like a disease on the world. They separate themselves from the rational order that governs all of us. The same nature that brings you whatever you face now is the same nature that brought you into existence. The person who stirs up trouble in the city is the one whose irrational actions pull their soul away from the one soul we all share as thinking beings.
original_excerpt: He is a true fugitive, that flies from reason, by which men are sociable. He blind, who cannot see with the eyes of his understanding. He poor, that stands in need of another, and hath not in himself all things needful for this life. He an aposteme of the world, who by being discontented with those things that happen unto him in the world, doth as it were apostatise, and separate himself from common nature's rational administration. For the same nature it is that brings this unto thee, whatsoever it be, that first brought thee into the world. He raises sedition in the city, who by irrational actions withdraws his own soul from that one and common soul of all rational creatures.

plain_english: One person says: 'I don't even have a coat, I don't even have a book, but I still practice philosophy. I'm half naked and have no bread to eat, yet I don't abandon reason.' But I say: I lack good teaching and instruction, yet I don't abandon reason either.
original_excerpt: There is, who without so much as a coat; and there is, who without so much as a book, doth put philosophy in practice. I am half naked, neither have I bread to eat, and yet I depart not from reason, saith one. But I say; I want the food of good teaching, and instructions, and yet I depart not from reason.

plain_english: Whatever skills and work you have learned, try to love them and find comfort in them. Live the rest of your life as someone who trusts the gods completely with himself and everything he has. As for other people, don't be a tyrant or a servant to anyone.
original_excerpt: What art and profession soever thou hast learned, endeavour to affect it, and comfort thyself in it; and pass the remainder of thy life as one who from his whole heart commits himself and whatsoever belongs unto him, unto the gods: and as for men, carry not thyself either tyrannically or servilely towards any.

plain_english: Think about the times of Vespasian, for example. You'll see the same things: people marrying, raising children, getting sick, dying, fighting, celebrating, doing business, farming, flattering others, bragging, being suspicious, scheming, wishing they were dead, complaining about their lives, courting lovers, hoarding money, chasing political office, seeking power. And isn't that whole era completely over and done? Now think about the times of Trajan. You see exactly the same things there too. And that age is also over and finished.
original_excerpt: Consider in my mind, for example's sake, the times of Vespasian: thou shalt see but the same things: some marrying, some bringing up children, some sick, some dying, some fighting, some feasting, some merchandising, some tilling, some flattering, some boasting, some suspecting, some undermining, some wishing to die, some fretting and murmuring at their present estate, some wooing, some hoarding, some seeking after magistracies, and some after kingdoms. And is not that their age quite over, and ended? Again, consider now the times of Trajan. There likewise thou seest the very self-same things, and that age also is now over and ended.

plain_english: Think about other times and whole nations in the same way. See how many people chased some worldly goal with everything they had, only to die soon after and return to dust. But especially remember the people you knew in your own lifetime. You watched them get completely caught up in pointless things. Meanwhile, they ignored what they should have been doing — the work their own nature demanded of them. Remember this: how much effort you put into something should match how important it really is. If you do this, you won't wear yourself out or get frustrated by spending too much time on small things.
original_excerpt: In the like manner consider other periods, both of times and of whole nations, and see how many men, after they had with all their might and main intended and prosecuted some one worldly thing or other did soon after drop away, and were resolved into the elements. But especially thou must call to mind them, whom thou thyself in thy lifetime hast known much distracted about vain things, and in the meantime neglecting to do that, and closely and unseparably (as fully satisfied with it) to adhere unto it, which their own proper constitution did require. And here thou must remember, that thy carriage in every business must be according to the worth and due proportion of it, for so shalt thou not easily be tired out and vexed, if thou shalt not dwell upon small matters longer than is fitting.

plain_english: Words that were once common and ordinary are now hard to understand and forgotten. The same thing happens to the names of people who were once famous. Camillus, Cæso, Volesius, Leonnatus — not long after, Scipio, Cato, then Augustus, then Hadrian, then Antoninus Pius. All these names will soon be outdated. They will seem like stories from another world. And I'm talking about men who once amazed their generations. As for everyone else, they die and their fame dies with them. So what will always be remembered? Nothing. It's all meaningless.
original_excerpt: Those words which once were common and ordinary, are now become obscure and obsolete; and so the names of men once commonly known and famous, are now become in a manner obscure and obsolete names. Camillus, Cæso, Volesius, Leonnatus; not long after, Scipio, Cato, then Augustus, then Adrianus, then Antoninus Pius: all these in a short time will be out of date, and, as things of another world as it were, become fabulous. And this I say of them, who once shined as the wonders of their ages, for as for the rest, no sooner are they expired, than with them all their fame and memory. And what is it then that shall always be remembered? all is vanity.

plain_english: What should we focus our care and effort on? Just this: that our thoughts and intentions are fair. That our actions help others. That we never lie. That we don't fool ourselves. That we're always ready to accept whatever happens to us as necessary, normal, ordinary — flowing from the same source that made both you and everything else. So give yourself over willingly to this chain of fate. Let the fates do with you what they will.
original_excerpt: What is it that we must bestow our care and diligence upon? even upon this only: that our minds and wills be just; that our actions be charitable; that our speech be never deceitful, or that our understanding be not subject to error; that our inclination be always set to embrace whatsoever shall happen unto us, as necessary, as usual, as ordinary, as flowing from such a beginning, and such a fountain, from which both thou thyself and all things are. Willingly therefore, and wholly surrender up thyself unto that fatal concatenation, yielding up thyself unto the fates, to be disposed of at their pleasure.

plain_english: Everything that exists right now, everything that has existed day by day — all the things we remember, and our minds and memories themselves — constantly think about this: all things exist through change and transformation. Get used to thinking about this often. The universe loves nothing more than changing the things that exist and making new things like them. So we can say that whatever exists is just the seed of what will come next. If you think that only what the earth or a womb receives is a seed, you're being too narrow in your thinking.
original_excerpt: Whatsoever is now present, and from day to day hath its existence; all objects of memories, and the minds and memories themselves, incessantly consider, all things that are, have their being by change and alteration. Use thyself therefore often to meditate upon this, that the nature of the universe delights in nothing more, than in altering those things that are, and in making others like unto them. So that we may say, that whatsoever is, is but as it were the seed of that which shall be. For if thou think that that only is seed, which either the earth or the womb receiveth, thou art very simple.

plain_english: You are ready to die, but you still haven't reached that perfect simplicity. You are still troubled by many things. You still worry about what might happen. You are not yet gentle enough with everyone. You have not yet become someone whose only focus is being just in everything you do.
original_excerpt: Thou art now ready to die, and yet hast thou not attained to that perfect simplicity: thou art yet subject to many troubles and perturbations; not yet free from all fear and suspicion of external accidents; nor yet either so meekly disposed towards all men, as thou shouldest; or so affected as one, whose only study and only wisdom is, to be just in all his actions.

plain_english: Look and see what state their minds are in. Those the world calls wise — see what they run from and fear, and what they chase after.
original_excerpt: Behold and observe, what is the state of their rational part; and those that the world doth account wise, see what things they fly and are afraid of; and what things they hunt after.

plain_english: Your suffering cannot exist in another person's mind or body. It cannot exist in your own body either, which is just the house where your soul lives. So where can it exist? Only in the part of you that forms ideas about misery. Don't let that part form such ideas, and you'll be fine. Even if your body gets cut, burned, corrupted, or rotten, let the part of you that judges these things stay calm. Let it judge this way: whatever happens equally to both good and bad people is neither good nor bad itself. What affects people who live well and people who live badly in the same way is neither natural nor unnatural. So it's neither good nor bad.
original_excerpt: In another man's mind and understanding thy evil Cannot subsist, nor in any proper temper or distemper of the natural constitution of thy body, which is but as it were the coat or cottage of thy soul. Wherein then, but in that part of thee, wherein the conceit, and apprehension of any misery can subsist? Let not that part therefore admit any such conceit, and then all is well. Though thy body which is so near it should either be cut or burnt, or suffer any corruption or putrefaction, yet let that part to which it belongs to judge of these, be still at rest; that is, let her judge this, that whatsoever it is, that equally may happen to a wicked man, and to a good man, is neither good nor evil. For that which happens equally to him that lives according to nature, and to him that doth not, is neither according to nature, nor against it; and by consequent, neither good nor bad.

plain_english: Think of the world as one living thing with one soul. All things flow into one shared awareness. Everything moves together as if guided by one mind making decisions. All things work together to cause each other's existence. Everything is connected in an endless chain.
original_excerpt: Ever consider and think upon the world as being but one living substance, and having but one soul, and how all things in the world, are terminated into one sensitive power; and are done by one general motion as it were, and deliberation of that one soul; and how all things that are, concur in the cause of one another's being, and by what manner of connection and concatenation all things happen.

plain_english: What are you, except for that better and divine part, but as Epictetus said well, a wretched soul appointed to carry a corpse up and down?
original_excerpt: What art thou, that better and divine part excepted, but as Epictetus said well, a wretched soul, appointed to carry a carcass up and down?

plain_english: Change itself cannot hurt you. And change cannot benefit you either. The age and time of the world is like a flood or fast river made up of all the things that happen. As soon as something appears and passes away, another thing takes its place. And that too will soon be gone.
original_excerpt: To suffer change can be no hurt; as no benefit it is, by change to attain to being. The age and time of the world is as it were a flood and swift current, consisting of the things that are brought to pass in the world. For as soon as anything hath appeared, and is passed away, another succeeds, and that also will presently out of sight.

plain_english: Whatever happens in the world is as natural and ordinary as roses blooming in spring or fruit ripening in summer. Sickness and death are the same. So are slander and betrayal. All these things that make fools happy or sad are just natural events. Whatever comes next always follows naturally from what came before. You must see the world's events not as random accidents or isolated necessities. See them as connected pieces that fit together in order and harmony. In the world's events, there is not just one thing after another. There is a beautiful pattern and connection.
original_excerpt: Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature, as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer. Of the same nature is sickness and death; slander, and lying in wait, and whatsoever else ordinarily doth unto fools use to be occasion either of joy or sorrow. That, whatsoever it is, that comes after, doth always very naturally, and as it were familiarly, follow upon that which was before. For thou must consider the things of the world, not as a loose independent number, consisting merely of necessary events; but as a discreet connection of things orderly and harmoniously disposed. There is then to be seen in the things of the world, not a bare succession, but an admirable correspondence and affinity.

plain_english: Keep Heraclitus in mind — that earth dies to become water, water dies to become air, air dies to become fire, and so on in reverse. Remember also the man who didn't know where his path led. Think about how reason governs everything in the world. We deal with reason constantly and intimately. Yet it's the very thing we fight against most. The things that happen to us every day still surprise us daily. We shouldn't speak or act like sleepwalkers, guided by opinions and fantasies. When we do that, we only think we're speaking and acting. And we shouldn't be like children who copy their fathers simply because "that's how we received it" — just following tradition without thinking.
original_excerpt: Let that of Heraclitus never be out of thy mind, that the death of earth, is water, and the death of water, is air; and the death of air, is fire; and so on the contrary. Remember him also who was ignorant whither the way did lead, and how that reason being the thing by which all things in the world are administered, and which men are continually and most inwardly conversant with: yet is the thing, which ordinarily they are most in opposition with, and how those things which daily happen among them, cease not daily to be strange unto them, and that we should not either speak, or do anything as men in their sleep, by opinion and bare imagination: for then we think we speak and do, and that we must not be as children, who follow their father's example; for best reason alleging their bare καθότι παρειλήφαμεν; or, as by successive tradition from our forefathers we have received it.

plain_english: Imagine one of the gods told you: You will die tomorrow, or the day after. Unless you were completely cowardly, you wouldn't think it was some great advantage to die the day after instead of tomorrow. What's the difference, really? For the same reason, it shouldn't matter much whether you die many years from now or the very next day.
original_excerpt: Even as if any of the gods should tell thee, Thou shalt certainly die to-morrow, or next day, thou wouldst not, except thou wert extremely base and pusillanimous, take it for a great benefit, rather to die the next day after, than to-morrow; (for alas, what is the difference!) so, for the same reason, think it no great matter to die rather many years after, than the very next day.

plain_english: Keep thinking about this: how many doctors who once looked so serious and frowned dramatically at their patients are now dead themselves. How many fortune-tellers who proudly predicted other people's deaths are gone. How many philosophers who wrote endless books about death and immortality have died. How many brave generals who killed so many others in battle are dead. How many kings and tyrants who cruelly abused their power over people's lives — as if they would live forever — are gone. And how many entire cities have vanished: Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and countless others.
original_excerpt: Let it be thy perpetual meditation, how many physicians who once looked so grim, and so theatrically shrunk their brows upon their patients, are dead and gone themselves. How many astrologers, after that in great ostentation they had foretold the death of some others, how many philosophers after so many elaborate tracts and volumes concerning either mortality or immortality; how many brave captains and commanders, after the death and slaughter of so many; how many kings and tyrants, after they had with such horror and insolency abused their power upon men's lives, as though themselves had been immortal; how many, that I may so speak, whole cities both men and towns: Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and others innumerable are dead and gone.

plain_english: Think about the people you have known who have died, one after another. This person buried that person, and soon after was buried himself. One after another, all in a short time. This is the truth: look at all worldly things as lasting only a day, and as worthless and contemptible. What is man? Just the other day he was conceived from something vile. In a few days he will be either an embalmed corpse or ashes. You must think about this according to truth and nature. Human life lasts only a moment. Accept this and depart peacefully and content, like a ripe olive that falls and praises the ground that held it and gives thanks to the tree that made it.
original_excerpt: Run them over also, whom thou thyself, one after another, hast known in thy time to drop away. Such and such a one took care of such and such a one's burial, and soon after was buried himself. So one, so another: and all things in a short time. For herein lieth all indeed, ever to look upon all worldly things, as things for their continuance, that are but for a day: and for their worth, most vile, and contemptible, as for example, What is man? That which but the other day when he was conceived was vile snivel; and within few days shall be either an embalmed carcass, or mere ashes. Thus must thou according to truth and nature, throughly consider how man's life is but for a very moment of time, and so depart meek and contented: even as if a ripe olive falling should praise the ground that bare her, and give thanks to the tree that begat her.

plain_english: You must be like a rocky cliff by the sea. The waves beat against it constantly, but the cliff stands firm. And around it, those angry waves grow still and quiet.
original_excerpt: Thou must be like a promontory of the sea, against which though the waves beat continually, yet it both itself stands, and about it are those swelling waves stilled and quieted.

plain_english: Poor me, this bad thing happened to me! No — lucky me. This thing happened, and I can handle it without falling apart. I'm not crushed by what's happening now. I'm not scared of what might come next. This could have happened to anyone. But not everyone could get through it without breaking down. So why call this bad luck instead of good luck? Can you really call something unlucky if it doesn't go against human nature? Can you call it a disaster if it doesn't work against what we're meant to do?
original_excerpt: Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened! nay, happy I, to whom this thing being happened, I can continue without grief; neither wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come. For as for this, it might have happened unto any man, but any man having such a thing befallen him, could not have continued without grief. Why then should that rather be an unhappiness, than this a happiness? But however, canst thou, O man! term that unhappiness, which is no mischance to the nature of man I Canst thou think that a mischance to the nature of man, which is not contrary to the end and will of his nature?

plain_english: What have you learned about human nature's purpose? Does what happened to you stop you from being just? Or brave? Or self-controlled? Or wise? Or careful? Or honest? Or humble? Or free? Or from having any of the other qualities that make human nature complete and satisfied? So remember this rule whenever you feel sorrow: whatever happened to you is not really a misfortune. To bear it with courage is true happiness.
original_excerpt: What then hast thou learned is the will of man's nature? Doth that then which hath happened unto thee, hinder thee from being just? or magnanimous? or temperate? or wise? or circumspect? or true? or modest? or free? or from anything else of all those things in the present enjoying and possession whereof the nature of man, (as then enjoying all that is proper unto her,) is fully satisfied? Now to conclude; upon all occasion of sorrow remember henceforth to make use of this dogma, that whatsoever it is that hath happened unto thee, is in very deed no such thing of itself, as a misfortune; but that to bear it generously, is certainly great happiness.

plain_english: This is a simple but powerful remedy against the fear of death. Think about those who greedily held onto life for a long time. What did they gain over those who died young? In the end, they all died too — Cadiciant, Fabius, Julianus Lepidus, and others who outlived many people, only to be buried themselves. The whole span of any life is short. And even that short time must be lived with troubles, difficult moods, and in a wretched body. So treat life as something that doesn't matter much either way. Look backward — you see an endless stretch of time before you were born. Look forward — you see endless time after you die. In all that infinity, what difference is there between living three days or three lifetimes?
original_excerpt: It is but an ordinary coarse one, yet it is a good effectual remedy against the fear of death, for a man to consider in his mind the examples of such, who greedily and covetously (as it were) did for a long time enjoy their lives. What have they got more, than they whose deaths have been untimely? Are not they themselves dead at the last? as Cadiciant's, Fabius, Julianus Lepidus, or any other who in their lifetime having buried many, were at the last buried themselves. The whole space of any man's life, is but little; and as little as it is, with what troubles, with what manner of dispositions, and in the society of how wretched a body must it be passed! Let it be therefore unto thee altogether as a matter of indifferency. For if thou shalt look backward; behold, what an infinite chaos of time doth present itself unto thee; and as infinite a chaos, if thou shalt look forward. In that which is so infinite, what difference can there be between that which liveth but three days, and that which liveth three ages?

plain_english: Always take the shortest path. The shortest path is the natural one: in everything you say and do, follow what is most sound and right. This approach will free you from all trouble, conflict, pretending, and showing off.
original_excerpt: Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect. For such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife, dissembling, and ostentation.
